name: HNSW Index
question: Can I hop through a graph to the nearest neighbours?
summary: HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) builds a layered graph. Upper layers are sparse with long links for coarse navigation; the bottom layer holds every vector with short links. A search enters at the top, greedily moves toward the query, and drops one layer at a time. It gives high recall at low latency and is the default index in most vector databases.
useCases: Low-latency, high-recall search where vectors fit in RAM
Data that grows continuously; no training step needed

items.detail: links per node; more = better recall, more memory (pgvector default 16)
candidate list while building; higher = better graph, slower build (default 64)
candidate list at query time; the main recall/latency dial (default 40)
assigned randomly per node; roughly log N layers

steps: Start with the defaults and measure recall on real queries
Tune ef_search at query time to reach your recall target
Budget memory: the graph links sit on top of the raw vectors
Expect slower builds and inserts than IVF
pitfalls: Memory-hungry: vectors and graph should fit in RAM
Heavy deletes and updates degrade the graph over time
Strict metadata filters can cut graph paths and lower recall
remember: Long hops on top, short hops at the bottom.
caption: Four hops and two layer drops reach the nearest vector without scanning the rest.

code.text: # Each added vector draws a random top layer: P(layer ≥ 1) = 1/M
index.set_ef(80)                  # ef_search: candidate list at query time
# Memory: vectors 5M × 384 × 4 B ≈ 7.7 GB; bottom-layer links 5M × 32 × 4 B ≈ 0.64 GB

steps.title: Set the graph parameters
steps.text: M = 16 links per node on the upper layers and 32 on the bottom. ef_construction = 200 sets how widely each insert searches for neighbours.

steps.title: Give each node a layer
steps.text: Each insert draws a random top layer. With M = 16, about 1 node in 16 reaches layer 1 and 1 in 256 reaches layer 2, so upper layers are sparse.

steps.title: Link each node to close neighbours
steps.text: On every layer it belongs to, a new node links to close nodes found by an ef_construction-wide search. The sparse top layer ends up with long links.

steps.title: Search greedily from the top
steps.text: The query enters at the top layer's entry point and hops to whichever neighbour is closer, until none is, then drops a layer and repeats.

steps.title: Widen the search on layer 0
steps.text: The bottom layer keeps a list of ef_search candidates instead of one, which recovers neighbours a purely greedy walk would miss. The best k are returned.

steps.title: Tune ef_search and budget memory
steps.text: Recall rises with ef_search and needs no rebuild. For 5 million 384-dim vectors, links add about 0.64 GB on top of 7.7 GB of vectors.

No training step, and it handles continuous inserts

goals: Explain how HNSW descends layers and why ef_search matters
Tune ef_search to a recall target before touching M
Estimate HNSW memory from vector count, dimensions and M

practice.scenario: A trading app's search-as-you-type must answer in under 50 ms. An HNSW index over 5 million vectors held in RAM, with ef_search raised from 40 to 80, meets both the latency and the recall target.

The default index in most vector databases

practice.analogy: Travelling by flight, then train, then auto-rickshaw: long hops to the right city, then shorter hops to the exact street.

library.name: pgvector (HNSW) or hnswlib
library.what: Same algorithm in SQL or in-process Python. Qdrant, Weaviate and Milvus use HNSW by default too.

samples.code:
CREATE INDEX ON chunks USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops)
  WITH (m = 16, ef_construction = 64);   -- pgvector defaults

SET hnsw.ef_search = 80;                 -- default 40; higher = better recall

SELECT id, body
FROM chunks
ORDER BY embedding <=> $1
LIMIT 10;

import hnswlib

index = hnswlib.Index(space="cosine", dim=384)
index.init_index(max_elements=5_000_000, M=16, ef_construction=200)
index.add_items(vectors, ids)            # vectors: (n, 384) float32

index.set_ef(80)                         # query-time recall / latency dial
labels, distances = index.knn_query(query_vec, k=10)

numericDrill.question: 1 million vectors with M = 16. The bottom layer keeps up to 2 × M = 32 links per node at 4 bytes each. Estimate the extra memory for those links, in MB.
numericDrill.answer: 32 links × 4 B × 1,000,000 nodes = 128 MB, on top of the raw vectors (1.5 GB at 384 float32 dims). Raising M raises this directly.

interview.question: Explain how HNSW search works.
interview.answer: Start at an entry point on the sparse top layer, greedily move to neighbours closer to the query, and when none is closer, drop a layer and repeat. The bottom layer holds every vector and is searched with a candidate list of size ef_search.

interview.question: What do M, ef_construction and ef_search trade off?
interview.answer: M sets links per node (recall and memory), ef_construction sets the build-time candidate list (graph quality versus build time), and ef_search sets the query-time list (recall versus latency). Only ef_search changes without a rebuild.

mistakes.mistake: Raising M to fix recall at query time
mistakes.fix: Tune ef_search first; M needs a rebuild

mistakes.mistake: Testing recall without your real filters
mistakes.fix: Benchmark with the filters production uses

quiz.question: An HNSW index gives recall@10 of 0.89 against a 0.95 target, and latency has headroom. What do you change first?
quiz.explanation: ef_search is the query-time dial and needs no rebuild.

quiz.question: A bank indexes 10 million 768-dimension float32 vectors with HNSW. How much RAM do the raw vectors need?
quiz.explanation: 768 × 4 B = 3,072 B per vector, and 3,072 B × 10 million ≈ 30.7 GB.

quiz.question: The same 10 million vectors use M = 16, so the bottom layer keeps up to 32 links per node at 4 bytes each. How much memory do those links add?
quiz.explanation: 32 × 4 B = 128 B per node, and 128 B × 10 million = 1.28 GB.

quiz.question: Which of these changes require rebuilding a pgvector HNSW index? Select all that apply.
quiz.explanation: m, ef_construction and the operator class are fixed at build time. ef_search is set per query or session.

quiz.question: With M = 16, about what share of nodes reaches layer 2?
quiz.explanation: Each layer up keeps about 1 in M nodes, so layer 2 has about 1 in 16 × 16 = 256.

quiz.question: What are pgvector’s default HNSW settings?
quiz.explanation: pgvector defaults to m = 16, ef_construction = 64 and hnsw.ef_search = 40.

quiz.question: Call-transcript embeddings arrive all day, and the topics shift from month to month. Why does HNSW suit this better than IVF?
options: It needs no training step; new vectors are linked in as they arrive
quiz.explanation: IVF depends on centroids learned at build time. HNSW inserts need no training, so drift does not stale the index.

quiz.question: A claims search filters to one branch (0.5% of rows) after the HNSW search, and returns 2 results instead of 10. What is the best fix?
options: Filter-aware search or iterative scans, or partitioning by branch
quiz.explanation: Post-filtering throws away almost every candidate. Filter during the search, scan iteratively, or partition by the filter.

quiz.question: Which of these increase the memory an HNSW index needs? Select all that apply.
quiz.explanation: Links grow with M and node count, and vectors grow with dimensions. ef_search only affects per-query work.

quiz.question: Which of these are known weaknesses of HNSW? Select all that apply.
options: Vectors and links must sit in RAM
Heavy deletes and updates degrade the graph
It needs k-means training before use
quiz.explanation: Memory, graph decay under churn and filtered search are the classic problems. HNSW has no training step.

quiz.question: An HNSW search over 5 million fare-rule vectors compares about 3,000 vectors per query. What share of the index is that?
Measurements: ef_search 40 gives recall 0.91 at 2.1 ms; 80 gives 0.96 at 3.4 ms; 160 gives 0.98 at 6.2 ms. The target is recall ≥ 0.95 with p95 under 5 ms. Which setting?
quiz.explanation: Only ef_search = 80 meets both the recall and the latency target.

quiz.question: Which practices make an HNSW benchmark trustworthy before launch? Select all that apply.
options: Measure recall against exact search on real queries
Measure p95 latency under concurrent load
Test on random vectors from a different dataset
quiz.explanation: Real queries, real filters and realistic load reflect production. Random vectors hide how your data clusters.

quiz.question: What happens when ef_construction is raised from 64 to 200?
options: A better-connected graph and a slower build
Faster queries at the same ef_search, with no other cost
quiz.explanation: A wider build-time search finds better neighbours for each insert, at the cost of build time.

quiz.question: A legal archive holds 2 million 1,536-dimension float32 vectors in HNSW with M = 16 (32 bottom-layer links of 4 B each). About how much RAM do vectors plus links need?
quiz.explanation: Vectors: 2 million × 6,144 B ≈ 12.29 GB. Links: 2 million × 128 B ≈ 0.26 GB. Total ≈ 12.5 GB.

quiz.question: Which pgvector pairing lets an HNSW index serve a cosine-distance query?
options: Any operator class works with any operator
quiz.explanation: The index operator class must match the ORDER BY operator: <=> is cosine distance and needs vector_cosine_ops.

quiz.question: A fraud team studies how an HNSW query runs. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
options: The search enters at the top layer
It moves greedily to closer neighbours
It drops a layer when no neighbour is closer
It scans every vector on layer 0
quiz.explanation: The bottom layer is explored with an ef_search-sized candidate list, not scanned in full.

quiz.question: An insurer has 400 million 768-dimension vectors (about 1.23 TB) and a server with 512 GB of RAM. What approach fits?
options: DiskANN, or heavy quantization, rather than full vectors in RAM
IVFFlat with all vectors in RAM
quiz.explanation: 400 million × 3,072 B ≈ 1.23 TB will not fit in 512 GB, so the full vectors must leave RAM or be compressed.

quiz.question: With M = 4, a graph needs a much larger ef_search to reach the same recall. Why?
options: Each node has few links, so greedy walks get stuck more easily
Vectors are stored at lower precision
ef_search is ignored when M is small
The graph uses a different distance metric
quiz.explanation: A poorly connected graph offers fewer routes to the query, so the search has to explore more candidates.

quiz.question: A Python service holds 2 million vectors in process and needs HNSW without a database. Which tool fits?
quiz.explanation: hnswlib is a fast in-process HNSW library for Python and C++.
